title: The Maggid's circle
hook: the Maggid of Mezeritch taught a circle of students who carried Hasidism across Eastern Europe

segments.voice: Yesterday, tikkun: holy sparks hidden in ordinary things. Your line was lift the sparks. Did one boring task get done with care? Day three hundred eleven.

Someone asks a Hasid what Torah he learned from his teacher. His answer, as Hasidim tell it: I didn't go to hear him teach Torah. I went to see how he laces and unlaces his boots. It sounds like a joke. It isn't. Not the lecture, but the way a person lives, down to the laces, can be the lesson. That teacher was the Maggid of Mezeritch, and the students who sat in his house would carry Hasidism across Eastern Europe.
screen: `WHAT TORAH DID YOU LEARN?` → `NOT THE LECTURE.` → `WATCHING HIM LACE HIS BOOTS.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Dov Ber was called the Maggid, which means the preacher, the one who tells. He was a serious scholar who came to the Baal Shem Tov, the tradition says, as something of a skeptic, and left as his disciple. After the Baal Shem Tov died, it was the Maggid who, as the tradition tells it, became the center of the movement. He wasn't a traveler. He was often ill, and he taught from his home in the small town of Mezeritch, in what is now Ukraine. But the students who came to him were extraordinary. Shneur Zalman of Liadi, who would found Chabad. Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, the defense attorney. Zusya of Anipoli, who worried about not being Zusya, and his brother Elimelech of Lizhensk. Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk, who later led a group of Hasidim to the Land of Israel. And many more. When the Maggid died, something unusual happened. There was no single heir. Instead, his students went out across Eastern Europe, and each became a teacher in his own place. One circle in one house turned into many Hasidic communities, each with its own melodies and customs. The opening mishnah of Pirkei Avot includes the charge: raise up many disciples. The Maggid did exactly that. His teaching didn't stay in Mezeritch. It went out the door, in the boots of his students.
screen: `MAGGID: THE ONE WHO TELLS.` · `A SMALL HOUSE IN MEZERITCH.` · `SHNEUR ZALMAN, LEVI YITZCHAK, ZUSYA.` · `NO SINGLE HEIR: MANY TEACHERS.` · then, large: `PASS IT ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pass on one thing you learned. Settle, and breathe. Think back over this year. Of everything you've heard, a story, a word, a saying, a practice, which one has stayed with you? Let it come. Now think of one person who might need it. Not as a lecture. The way the Maggid's students carried him: by how they lived. How could you pass this on, in a sentence, or in the way you act today? If you pray, you can give thanks for whoever taught you. The bell holds the time.
The Maggid's circle. The students of Dov Ber of Mezeritch, who went home after his death and carried Hasidism across Eastern Europe.
Your line: pass it on. Today, share one thing you've learned with someone who might need it, in a word or in the way you live it. Day three hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Many Hasidic communities trace their lineage back through their founding rebbe to the Maggid of Mezeritch and the Baal Shem Tov, and they retell the Maggid's teachings at gatherings and on the anniversary of his death.

fork.setup: your teacher, the Maggid, has died. there's no single successor. what do his students do?
options: choose one of them to lead everyone.
go home and each become a teacher in his own place.
close the circle and stop teaching.
fork.reveal: they scattered across Eastern Europe, and one house in Mezeritch became many Hasidic communities.

original.note: Hebrew: preacher, one who tells. From the root that also gives Haggadah, the telling.

trapdoor: what you thought: a teacher and his fan club.
what it means: a circle of students who carried one teacher's way of life across a continent.
what a scholar hears: after the Maggid's death Hasidic leadership decentralized into regional dynasties founded by the Maggid's disciples, the shape Hasidism still has today.

sources.ref: Traditions about Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezeritch, and his disciples

notes: The boots saying is usually attributed to Rabbi Leib, son of Sarah (Leib Saras); the script leaves him unnamed. Confirm.
Dates: Baal Shem Tov d. 1760; Maggid d. 1772; Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk's aliyah 1777 (not dated in the script). Confirm.
Zusya and Elimelech as brothers and both disciples of the Maggid: confirm.
The Maggid's first meeting with the Baal Shem Tov 'as something of a skeptic' follows tradition; confirm.
Haggadah and maggid share the root n-g-d: confirm for the original-language note.

Review pass: historians debate how far the Maggid was the Baal Shem Tov's single successor (the early movement had several centers), so 'became the center of the movement' is now framed 'as the tradition tells it'. 'The first line of Pirkei Avot' changed to 'the very first teaching' (raise many disciples is the second of three sayings in Avot 1:1). The list of regions (incl. Lithuania) is approximate for the disciples' later seats; confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Think of' or tells the listener what they remember; cut the stock 'put it perfectly'; dropped uncited dates (1760, 1772) from voice, fork and trapdoor, and 'dozens'/'many of which still exist'; Avot 1:1 now described accurately (the charge is one of three sayings in the opening mishnah); the approximate list of regions removed.
